A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same d2 research framework. The complete main texts and Appendices A–E, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and matchable despite the changed title, numbering, and layout.

before.justification: v3 reports original toxicity-steering experiments, reasoning benchmark results, and ablations. Appendix D includes additional finetuning and reinforcement-learning results.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds Qwen3 and Dream experiments and coding evaluations. Table 5 explicitly distinguishes the authors' new RL results from previously published SFT results.

M1.justification: The GRPO objectives, AnyOrder sequence packing and attention rules, and StepMerge trajectory segmentation remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–4 retain the same procedures. The additional model applications introduce no new method component.

E1.justification: v4 adds HumanEval and MBPP code-generation evaluations, substantially extending evaluation beyond mathematics, logical reasoning, and toxicity steering. Code-related distillation prompts already appeared in v3, but these coding benchmarks are new. The original task coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 Table 5 adds Block diffusion SFT and AO SFT reference comparisons for Qwen3, reporting 48% and 62% GSM8K accuracy from Arriola and Kuleshov. The existing RL comparator set is retained. AGRPO is newly discussed but is not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The experimental design expands to Qwen3-1.7B and Dream 7B, with Dream evaluated zero-shot. New coding experiments use StepMerge N=16, train at length 256, evaluate at lengths 256 and 512, and report best checkpoints under matched FLOPs. These are additional experimental settings; the retained experiments' Appendix C settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 8 adds a focused length-generalization test asking whether coding policies trained at length 256 retain performance at length 512. The earlier exact-versus-approximate likelihood, StepMerge N-sensitivity, and finetuning-data ablations remain unchanged, including their appendix evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the experimental results. The existing point-estimate reporting and averaging over 512 toxicity samples are retained; the new tables introduce no uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results and plotted curves are retained, but v4 adds substantial results in Tables 5, 7, and 8. Examples include Qwen3 GSM8K accuracy of 67% versus 63% for diffu-GRPO; Dream Sudoku/GSM8K accuracy of 0.91/0.80 versus 0.79/0.73; and length-512 HumanEval/MBPP scores of 40.9/45.5 versus 34.8/41.6. These are newly reported experiments, not same-setting improvements over v3.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 and the definitions, assumptions, derivations, and proofs in Appendix A are unchanged. The added connection to composite likelihood provides conceptual motivation without introducing a new formal result.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a trajectory-based GRPO framework, exact one-pass estimation for compatible any-order models, bounded approximate estimation through StepMerge, and leading results on the same four reasoning benchmarks without supervised chain-of-thought finetuning. The estimator-family framing restates these contributions without changing their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v4 links the coding results to improved length generalization, revises discussion of emerging any-order models' applicability, and adds an Impact Statement connecting toxicity steering to harmful reward-driven generation. The coding interpretation needs qualification: despite the statement that StepMerge maintains or improves performance, Table 8 shows MBPP declining from 45.9 to 45.5 at the longer length.

D1.justification: v4 identifies the additional model checkpoints and documents coding-specific details, including N=16, training and evaluation lengths, and reuse of Zhao et al.'s training and reward recipe. Existing appendix hyperparameters, pseudocode, FLOP formulas, asset disclosures, and the project code-access statement remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 connects StepMerge to composite likelihood through Besag, Lindsay, and Varin et al., adds coding-benchmark references, and distinguishes its deterministic estimator from AGRPO's Monte Carlo approach. The former anonymous Set Diffusion citation is identified as Arriola and Kuleshov; numerous other citation changes update publication metadata rather than introduce different works.

P1.justification: The title and targeted passages in the abstract, introduction, method overview, and conclusion emphasize trajectory likelihood estimation and the two target model classes. v4 also adds a contents listing, a Set Diffusion subsection, and an Impact Statement. Most prose and the established section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v4 adds an estimator-summary table and three result tables: Tables 1, 5, 7, and 8. Existing tables are renumbered and displays reflow, with some figures resized or relocated. All twelve original figures are retained; the overall main-text and appendix layout conventions remain stable.

improvement.justification: The additional backbone, coding, and length-generalization experiments strengthen evidence for applicability beyond v3's original evaluations. The estimator summary and specific dual-use discussion also improve clarity and context. The gains are tempered by brief documentation of the new experiments, unchanged absence of run-to-run uncertainty, and the slightly overstated MBPP length interpretation. Overall, these are useful improvements to an already established method and evidence base.
